Replacing Worn Turf in Meadow Woods

Turf replacement in Meadow Woods, tearing out a worn system, correcting the base and laying new material, prices close to a new residential install minus whatever base can be reused, rather than a flat per-square-foot rate.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Turf from the community's growth years is reaching the end of its life

Meadow Woods added more than 14,000 residents between 2000 and 2010, and any turf installed during that stretch of construction and the years right after is now old enough to sit inside, or past, the lower end of a synthetic system's typical 10-to-20-year lifespan. UV exposure, foot traffic and whatever infill was used all decide where a given yard actually falls in that range, but a system installed before Florida's current material standard took effect in 2026 is also worth checking against today's rules on infill and backing before assuming a like-for-like swap is the right call.

Thirty-year-old irrigation lines under a yard about to be redone

A home built during Meadow Woods' 1990s wave of construction is now old enough that its original irrigation system is approaching three decades in the ground, and a full turf replacement is the natural point to deal with it properly rather than working around it again. Any head still live under the footprint gets capped as part of the state's turf standard regardless of the line's age, but a replacement job is also the easier moment to have a plumber confirm the rest of that aging system isn't leaking into the base before new rock goes down on top of it.

Working a base rebuild around plantings that stayed put

Mature landscaping installed after the original turf went in, a hedge line, a paver walkway added later, can box in how much of a Meadow Woods lawn's base gets fully rebuilt during a replacement versus how much gets corrected in place. A section running close to an established root system or a fixed hardscape edge sometimes gets recompacted and regraded rather than fully excavated, while an open area with nothing constraining it gets torn out completely. The base plan for a replacement has to work around what's changed on the lot since the first install, not just what the original footprint assumed.

Scheduling a rebuild around the rainy season's compaction window

Base material compacts properly only when it's reasonably dry, so a Meadow Woods replacement scheduled during the June-through-September rainy season needs tighter weather windows than the same job in a drier month, sometimes splitting demo and base work across a few days to catch dry stretches between afternoon storms. A replacement planned for the dry season has more flexibility, which is one reason timing a full tear-out and rebuild around the calendar, not just around a homeowner's availability, affects how smoothly the job actually goes.

Say you have a 1,100 sq ft lawn installed during the 2000s

Say you have a 1,100 sq ft backyard lawn installed sometime during Meadow Woods' 2000s growth years, now showing thin infill, a couple of open seams and a base that's started to hold water after storms. There's no flat per-square-foot number for that kind of job the way there is for a first-time install, since the price depends heavily on how much of the existing base can be reused versus rebuilt. A base that's still draining and holding grade keeps the job closer to a straightforward resurface; a base that's settled unevenly pushes the price close to what a brand-new install on that same footprint would cost.

Choosing a PFAS-free product during a replacement

Florida's turf standard bars intentionally added PFAS in any new synthetic turf installation, and a Meadow Woods homeowner replacing an older lawn gets to choose from current product lines built to that standard rather than whatever was on the market when the original turf went in. Asking a supplier for documentation on this point during a replacement is a reasonable ask, since it's exactly the kind of material change a full re-turf is positioned to address that a smaller repair job never would be.

How much of the old base actually gets reused

Replacing turf on Meadow Woods' flat, poorly drained flatwoods soil usually means opening up the base to check it, not just pulling the surface material and relaying new turf on what's there. A base that's held its grade and still drains well can often be topped up and re-compacted; one that's settled unevenly, which is more common on this area's poorly drained soil after 15 to 20 years, needs a fuller rebuild. That distinction is most of what separates a lower-cost replacement from one that prices close to a brand-new install.

Rebuilding the same footprint that never should have qualified

A Meadow Woods lawn's original layout sometimes sits inside a live oak's drip line, or closer than ten feet to a pond or canal without a seawall or bulkhead between them, footprints that wouldn't meet the current standard if proposed fresh today. Rebuilding to the exact same footprint during a replacement carries that same problem forward into a brand-new install rather than correcting it, when a replacement is specifically the moment a footprint like that can be adjusted without the added cost of a standalone project.

Keeping the new spec sheet for the next replacement cycle

The product spec sheet and invoice from a Meadow Woods replacement are worth keeping somewhere easy to find, not just for an HOA that might ask again, but for whoever handles the next replacement ten to twenty years from now, since knowing exactly what backing, infill, and base depth went in saves a round of guessing when that lawn eventually needs the same decision made again. A folder with the paperwork from this job is a small thing that saves real time on the next one.

Questions people ask

Is turf installed in Meadow Woods during the 2000s boom safe to just resurface?

Sometimes. If the base has held its grade and still drains well, a resurface can work. If it's settled unevenly, which is common after 15 to 20 years on this area's poorly drained soil, a fuller rebuild is the more reliable fix.

Does replacing turf trigger the state's newer infill rules on an older Meadow Woods lawn?

A replacement is a new install for practical purposes, so it should meet the current state standard on infill and backing even if the original system predated the 2026 rule.
